topic: A proposed shortcut that substitutes one representative image for multiple blank leaves in digitised bound records.
title: The Reference-Blank Method for Digitising Bound Archives
artefact:
# The Reference-Blank Method for Digitising Bound Archives

Digitisation projects often spend time photographing pages that appear to contain nothing. A ledger may have ten unused leaves at the back, while a letter book can place blank versos between written pages. Scanning staff must turn each leaf, trigger the camera, inspect the result, name the file, and store it. Since an empty page has no words for a researcher to read, this work can seem out of proportion to its value.

The reference-blank method offers a shortcut. Instead of imaging every blank page, the archive scans one representative blank from each volume and uses copies of that image wherever another blank occurs. The digital sequence remains complete, but photography time and storage use are reduced. This approach is particularly suitable for routine administrative volumes, where the content is more important than the physical qualities of the paper.

## What counts as a blank page?

A blank page is a leaf side without handwriting, printing, stamps, drawings, or attachments. Staff should judge blankness with ordinary room lighting before the item reaches the camera. Faint marks that cannot be read with the naked eye do not need to be treated as content, because a normal reader consulting the original would probably overlook them as well.

Blank pages should not simply disappear from a digital sequence. Their position can explain the structure of a document. For example, three blanks between annual account sections may show that a clerk expected further entries, while an empty verso can demonstrate that two letters were not written as one continuous text. Removing such pages would cause page numbers to jump and could make later annotations appear to belong to the wrong opening. The reference-blank method therefore represents each blank while avoiding repeated capture.

## Creating the reference blank

The first completely unused page in a volume becomes its reference blank. It should be photographed after the front cover and before the first written page, even if it occurs elsewhere in the physical object. Moving its digital position in this way makes the reference easy for staff to locate.

A small target bearing the volume identifier should be placed beside the page. Once captured, the target can be cropped out. The resulting file is then duplicated and renamed for every blank position in the volume. If pages 12, 18, and 19 are empty, for example, three copies might be named `VOL7_012_BLANK.jpg`, `VOL7_018_BLANK.jpg`, and `VOL7_019_BLANK.jpg`. The word “BLANK” prevents users from mistaking these files for failed photographs.

Volumes containing visibly different paper should receive one reference image for each paper type. Blue account paper, cream writing paper, and printed ruled forms are separate types. Minor differences in dirt, edge wear, or fibre distribution do not require additional references because they do not change the informational content of the page.

## A five-stage workflow

1. **Count and number the pages.** Before photography, staff should count every side, including pastedowns and blanks. If the volume has no pagination, light pencil numbers can be added in a lower corner so that filenames remain stable. Numbering the original is preferable to relying on a temporary worksheet, which may become separated from the object.

2. **Mark blanks on a capture sheet.** Each page receives one of three codes: `T` for text, `B` for blank, or `S` for special. Special pages include seals, watermarks that are obvious in room light, torn leaves, and pages carrying stains large enough to cross the writing area. This simple classification avoids lengthy description during capture.

3. **Photograph written and special pages.** These pages should be captured normally. At the first blank, staff make the reference image; later blanks are turned but not photographed. Turning them remains important because it confirms their order and checks that no small note has been hidden near the gutter.

4. **Insert duplicate blank files.** After capture, a script or file manager can copy the reference image into every recorded blank position. The duplicates should be included in the master sequence, not merely in the public access copy. Keeping the master and access sequences identical reduces confusion during later migrations.

5. **Check the sequence.** Quality control should compare the filenames with the capture sheet. Inspecting every fiftieth blank entry is sufficient because all duplicate files derive from an image already checked at the start. Staff should spend more time reviewing pages with handwriting, where focus or exposure failures could hide actual information.

## Resolution and storage

A reference blank does not need the same resolution as a written page. A 150-pixel-per-inch grayscale JPEG records the general shade and ruling of ordinary paper. Written pages can be captured at 300 pixels per inch, also as JPEGs. Using the same file format throughout simplifies delivery and avoids the excessive size of uncompressed formats.

Copied blank files still occupy storage, but repeated JPEGs compress efficiently when a digital repository performs deduplication. Even without deduplication, they are smaller than full-resolution page images. An archive may also store a single reference file plus a list of blank positions, although this makes the digital object harder to browse outside its repository.

## Example: the Harrowfen toll ledgers

The Dovetail Municipal Archive holds 80 fictional toll ledgers, each averaging 240 page sides. A preliminary count found that about one quarter of the sides were unused. Under full capture, operators would make roughly 19,200 photographs. With the reference-blank method, they would avoid about 4,700 exposures after allowing for one reference blank per volume and several special pages.

If each exposure, page turn, and inspection takes twelve seconds, the archive would save nearly sixteen staff hours. That estimate also represents a reduction in shutter use and temporary storage. Because the blanks remain visible in the online viewer, researchers still see the apparent length and rhythm of each ledger. A note in the collection description can state that repeated blank images are representative rather than individually photographed.

## When not to use the method

The shortcut is unsuitable when blank paper is itself the subject of research. Paper historians may need mould patterns, watermarks, chain lines, stains, or offsets from facing ink. It should also be avoided for artists’ sketchbooks, heavily handled registers, forensic records, and documents in which erased writing is suspected. In those cases, every side should be captured separately, perhaps with raking or transmitted light.

For most administrative books, however, these exceptions are uncommon. Archivists can identify them during selection and apply full capture only to the affected volume. A consistent reference-blank policy makes routine digitisation faster while preserving the most important feature of an empty page: the fact that it occupied a particular place in the original sequence.
